solution: $f(x)=x^{2}+e^{x}\int_0^x e^{-t}f(t)dt$, so $f(0)=0$; $f$ is differentiable (right side is)
solution_full: Take $e^{x}$ out of the integral: $f(x)=x^{2}+e^{x}\int_0^{x}e^{-t}f(t)\,dt$. Putting $x=0$ gives $f(0)=0$.
The right side is differentiable (product of $e^{x}$ and an integral of a continuous function), so $f$ is differentiable.
By the Newton-Leibniz rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\int_0^{x}e^{-t}f(t)\,dt=e^{-x}f(x)$. Hence $f'(x)=2x+e^{x}\int_0^xe^{-t}f(t)dt+e^{x}\cdot e^{-x}f(x)$.
From the given equation, $e^{x}\int_0^xe^{-t}f(t)dt=f(x)-x^{2}$. So $f'(x)=2x+f(x)-x^{2}+f(x)$, i.e. $f'-2f=2x-x^{2}$.
This is a linear differential equation. Try $f_p=ax^{2}+bx+c$: $2ax+b-2ax^{2}-2bx-2c=-x^{2}+2x$ gives $a=\frac12$, $b=-\frac12$, $c=-\frac14$.
Check: this $f$ satisfies the original integral equation (verified by direct integration).
originality_note: New: an integral equation with the kernel e^{x-t} and a forcing x^2, whose differentiation feeds the integral back through the equation itself (way 5). Closest known: textbook equations f(x) = e^x + int_0^x e^{-t} f(x-t) dt. Different because: the kernel depends on x and must be factored out before differentiating, and the resulting DE has a polynomial forcing.
